title: What does a 1:N model of a cargo UAV tell you about the 1:1 aircraft?
lede: research programme (proposal stage): per-quantity error budget for a Froude-scaled cargo aircraft model, with a stdlib scaling calculator; first-order result: at 1:10 the model needs 17 to 35% more power than Froude scaling predicts
summary: An open research programme on sub-scale flight testing of cargo and delivery aircraft. Dynamic (Froude) scaling keeps trim, mode frequencies and gust response, but Reynolds number falls as n<sup>1.5</sup>, so skin friction rises, and cell, motor and propeller performance do not scale with the airframe. The programme asks how large each error is for 1:2 to 1:20 models of an electric cargo aircraft, and whether a corrected model can recover it. Milestone 1 is a stdlib calculator (9 tests; exponent table dimensionally checked, ISA and Sutherland values checked) and a first-order flat-plate result for a 1,000 kg, aspect-ratio-10 airframe: at 1:10 the model needs 1.27× the Froude-scaled power (1.17 to 1.35 across form-factor, wetted-area and aspect-ratio sweeps) and L/D falls from 22.8 to 18.0. An untripped laminar-flow variant makes small models look better than full size, which is a modelling artefact and the reason the next milestones use XFOIL polars measured against UIUC data. The airframe constants are design choices, not a specific aircraft; the Froude exponents and the NASA TP-1435 and other citations are from memory and were not machine-checked (registries returned 403). Preliminary. Milestone 6a: on 134 measured cruise flights of a DJI Matrice 100 (Rodrigues et al. 2022 data, CC BY 4.0), electrical power scales with takeoff mass to the power 1.54 (95% bootstrap interval 1.41 to 1.67 over flights), consistent with the m<sup>1.5</sup> behind Froude power n<sup>3.5</sup>, within one airframe and a 13.6% mass range; electrical cruise power is 1.85× the ideal induced power at every payload, and falls 10% from 4 to 12 m/s. Payload is partly confounded with flight day (density not logged). Milestone 7a: at n = 0.2 the uncorrected model needs 1.157× the Froude power; a search of 178 section and boundary-layer cases (NACA 4-digit and low-Reynolds sections, CL within 6%, lift-curve slope within 5%) reaches at best 1.086, so no section restores it to within 5% (H5 refuted in this space; NeuralFoil polars, similarity kept). Milestone 11a (airspace): for one delivery hub in Manhattan with 17,250 measured destinations (NYC Uber pickups, April 2014; CC BY 4.0), 20 m/s cruise and a 50 m separation radius, en-route losses of separation per flight grow linearly with traffic and reach 0.1 per flight at 62 flights/h in one layer. A closed form derived from the radial geometry, C = (λ<sup>2</sup>/v) E[min(2 min(d<sub>1</sub>, d<sub>2</sub>), R / sin(Δφ/2))], matches an exact closest-approach simulator within 1% in the base case and within 4.3% in 89 of 90 sweep comparisons. Manhattan's narrow bearings double the conflicts; the gas model is 7× low (17× at 10 km); separate outbound and inbound layers remove 95%. Speed and separation radius swept, not sourced; no wind or other operators. Milestone 11b (wind): a generalised closed form (within 1.7% of the simulator in 8 base cases) shows wind raises one layer’s en-route conflicts by about as much as it lengthens time aloft, v/H = √(1 − w<sup>2</sup> sin<sup>2</sup>β)/(1 − w<sup>2</sup>); over 4,392 measured ERA5 100 m wind hours (NYC, Apr to Sep 2014) the average hour adds 6.1% at 20 m/s (10.0% at 15, 2.7% at 30), and the outbound/inbound layer split still leaves under 1% at equal airspeeds. Steady wind per hour; preliminary. Milestone 11c (several hubs and operators): one operator’s nearest-hub flights never cross (zero cross-hub conflicts; en-route conflicts per flight fall from 0.40 to 0.023 going from 1 to 8 hubs at 240 flights/h); with four overlapping operators 31.5% of en-route conflicts are crossings, a closed form with a crossing term matches the simulator within 7.4%, and the semicircular altitude rule leaves 68% fewer en-route conflicts than an outbound/inbound split. Straight legs, equal speeds, k-means operator sites; preliminary. Milestone 11e (which bit to spend extra altitude layers on): with four overlapping operators, separating the operators whose service areas overlap most, on top of the semicircular rule, leaves 2.3× to 3.7× fewer en-route conflicts than separating outbound from inbound legs, and a speed band does worse than leg direction; the closed form picks a tied-best assignment in all three scenarios. Leg direction still wins once conflicts within 250 m of a hub are counted. Illustrative speeds and shares; preliminary. Milestone 11f (eight operators, which share a layer): max-cut on closed-form pairwise conflict weights picks the simulator’s best of all 127 two-group splits in all three scenarios and, on top of the semicircular rule, leaves 20% to 29% of its en-route conflicts; max-cut on market share over hub distance is within 2.2% with no traffic model, a demand-overlap split is 1.3× to 1.6× worse and a speed split 1.5× to 2.7× worse. Illustrative speeds and shares; preliminary. Milestone 11g (24 random layouts, mixed radii, speeds and shares): the closed-form max-cut stays within 1.6% of the simulator’s best split in all 24, while the hub-distance heuristic is at least 5% worse in 19 of 24 (median 1.14×, worst 1.75×), so 11f’s near-free heuristic held only for equal-radius operators. Swept, not sourced; preliminary. Milestone 11h (layers on paper): a kinetic-gas grid integral with each operator’s flights spread uniformly over its service disc, needing no traffic data, lands a median 2.6% above the closed form’s split against 13.6% for hub distance, at a fifteenth of the compute; the same integral on the real destinations reproduces the closed form, so the rest of the gap is the demand map. Swept, not sourced; preliminary. Milestone 11i (land mask): spreading customers over the city’s land instead of the whole disc brings the paper split within 5% of the closed form in 17 of 24 layouts (13 without), median excess 1.9% against 2.6%, but leaves the pair ranking unchanged, so the missing demand information is density on land, not the water. Milestone 11j (census demand): weighting each operator’s customers by LODES 2022 jobs fixes the paper weights’ pair ranking (median Pearson r against the simulator 0.990 against 0.964, worst 0.948 against 0.692) and their scale (total 1.01× the closed form’s), but not the split it picks: median excess 1.2%, within 5% in 17 of 24. Residents plus jobs reaches median 1.000, within 5% in 18 of 24, never worse than jobs alone (6 better, sign test p = 0.03, not pre-registered); 2020 residents alone do no better than the land mask. Five of nine predictions refuted; preliminary. Milestone 11k (robust selection): hedging against pair-weight error does not fix the paper split’s misses. Voting over perturbed weights gives a mean excess of 2.9% against 3.3% (2 layouts better, 2 worse, p = 1.0), and the largest misses sit where the paper weight is most confident (Spearman +0.33), so the error is bias, not near-ties. The simulator’s best split is in the paper top 5 in 21 of 24 layouts: rank on paper, then simulate five. Preliminary. Milestone 11l (simulation budget): in this pair-separable simulator a short run of 20,000 flights (0.31 CPU s, a tenth of the full run and cheaper than the paper integral) picks a split a mean 1.2% above the closed form’s, within 5% in 67 of 72 runs, against 3.3% for the paper argmax. Restricting a short run to the paper’s top five helps only at 5,000 to 10,000 flights (mean 1.9% against 3.8% at 5,000, sign test p = 0.02) and hurts from 50,000 up, because the top five miss the best split in 3 of 24 layouts; for a simulator that needs one run per candidate, the paper’s top 10 at 20,000 flights gives 1.0% for 3 CPU s against 39 s for all 127. Three of eight predictions refuted; preliminary. Milestone 11m (whose demand is wrong): in 5 of the 6 layouts where the census paper split misses by more than 5%, replacing one operator’s census map with its real destinations fixes it (layout 0: 1.213 to 0.997; layout 17: 1.103 to 1.000), and one pair weight carries 81% and 100% of the error in those two; neither leg-length nor whole-disc mismatch predicts the culprit (Spearman −0.15, 0.19), and a leg-length rescale does nothing. Preliminary. Milestone 11n (disclosure order): asking operators for real destination data in order of traffic share puts the paper split within 5% of the closed form in 22 of 24 layouts after one disclosure; a census-only influence order gets all 24 after four (mean excess 0.2%), against eight for a random order; one well-chosen disclosure would always suffice, but more disclosure is not monotone (13 of 24 layouts have a subset more than 2% worse than one of its own subsets). Preliminary. Milestone 11o (stopping rule): stopping share-ordered disclosure once the paper split stops changing uses a mean 1.5 disclosures for a mean excess of 0.9% (22 of 24 within 5%), with no simulation; a 20,000-flight simulation guard adds noise rather than removing it (1.2%), and the rule needs two unchanged disclosures under the influence order. Preliminary. Milestone 11p (sized guard): neither a combined share/influence asking order nor a pooled 100,000-flight check improves the stopping rule (both stay at a mean 0.9% excess); a post-hoc check shows why: a 20,000-flight run measures the ratio of two candidate splits with a 5% to 6% standard deviation, so separating a 2% gap needs roughly 560,000 to 830,000 flights, and per-layout differences below about 2% are within the 200,000-flight scoring run’s own noise. Preliminary. Milestone 11q (1M-flight reference): re-scoring the headline rules on five new 200,000-flight runs per layout moves every mean by 0.3% or less and keeps their order (real-map paper split 1.000, stopping rule 1.006, census-only 1.031); the best split on the single scoring run was a winner’s curse (0.998 in-sample, 1.002 on the reference), and some single-layout misses shrank into the noise (layout 16: 6.7% to 2.5% ± 2.6%). Preliminary. Milestone 11r (exact timing): integrating the Poisson launch times out analytically gives an unbiased estimator of the simulator’s expected conflicts (pooled ratio 1.0005 over 24 layouts) that is only about 1.5× more efficient per CPU second; it shows 11d’s closed form undercounts en-route conflicts by 7% (3% to 12%) yet ranks operator pairs almost exactly (r ≥ 0.998), so its layer split is within 0.05% of the exact optimum in 22 of 24 layouts and within 0.35% in the other two. Preliminary. Milestone 11t computes the missing take-off and turnaround term exactly from hub sites and destination lists, with no sampled flight pairs: it is the same in every altitude layer, grows as πR<sup>2</sup>, comes 60% from drones turning for home at delivery points and 40% from hub launches, and brings the closed form within 2% of the exact estimator in all 24 layouts (mean 1.0025). It does not reduce the estimate’s noise and is about 5× slower than sampling in pure Python. Preliminary. Milestone 11u evaluates that term on 100 m paper-weight grids from destination maps: it matches the exact term to 0.7% at 14× less compute and lifts the paper weights’ level from 0.93 to 1.01 of the exact estimator, without changing any layer-split decision; census-only uniform maps give 0.44 of it. Preliminary. Milestone 11v computes that term from public census maps instead: residents plus jobs give 0.83 of the exact term (uniform discs 0.44), lift the census paper weights from 0.88 to 0.94 of the exact estimator, and fix one of their bad layer splits (9% to 0.04%) without changing any other. Preliminary. Milestone 11w fits a residents/jobs mix for both terms, holding each layout out: about 89% jobs brings the census level to 0.98 of exact out of sample, but no better per layout than one scale factor, so the census error left is layout-specific. Preliminary. Milestone 11x sums the flux term exactly over destination pairs, so the whole closed form needs no sampled flight pairs (130 s per layout): against it, the 400,000-pair estimates used since 11g carry about 0.8% heavy-tailed noise, enough to pick a layer split up to 2.75% worse in 5 of 24 layouts. Preliminary. Milestone 11y makes the exact closed form about 3× faster (50 CPU s per layout instead of 143 s) with the same numbers to 1.6×10<sup>−15</sup> and the same layer splits: crossing tests pruned by angle (2.2×) and a symmetric same-operator sum (9.6×, added post hoc); angle pruning alone, as pre-registered, gave 1.44×. Preliminary. Milestone 11z re-scores 15 planner rules’ layer splits from 11g to 11w against that exact closed form: every mean loss moves by under 1% and no rule changes rank (hub distance 19%, census maps 2.6% to 3.2%, real destination maps 0.1% above the best split), but the two sampled references shared one draw that hid a 2.75% miss on one layout. Preliminary. Milestone 11aa sums the simulator’s exact expected conflict rate over every pair of destinations, with no sampled flights: the closed form is 0.26% high on average (all 24 layouts within 1.4%), ranks operator pairs exactly, and picks the simulator’s best layer split in all 24 layouts; 11z’s rule rankings hold to within 0.09%. Preliminary. Milestone 11ab tests the planner rules on 72 fresh layouts, against that simulator-checked closed form: a 100 m raster of the operators’ real destinations picks the best of 127 layer splits in 65 of 72 and loses 0.15% on average (worst 4.2%) at about 1/30 of the closed form’s cost; census maps lose 1.4% to 2.0%, uniform discs 5.8%, hub distance 14%, the same order as on 11z’s 24 layouts. 11ac repeats it with 12 and 16 operators (2,047 and 32,767 splits): the destination raster picks the best split in 21 and 16 of 24 layouts and loses at most 0.44%, while a two-layer split itself is worth less as operators are added (the average split is only 1.5 to 1.6× the best, against 2.0 with eight). Milestone 11ad adds layer groups: the best four groups leave 7.6% (12 operators) and 8.7% (16) of the en-route conflict weight in shared layers, against a third with two, and eight groups come close to the operators’ own self-conflicts; the destination raster finds those partitions within 0.2%, while adding the second group bit by splitting each half again costs 15% more conflicts than re-planning all four groups. Extra climb through the added bands is not charged. 11ai charges altitude-keeping error between neighbouring levels: with a 25 ft separation and 1 m error per drone the best spacing is 13.3 m (5 bands under 400 ft, not 8), and flying 25 ft levels as if altitude were exact multiplies losses of separation by 4 to 5; separation and error are swept, not sourced. 11aj mixes barometric and GNSS altitude references: with a 3 m mismatch between them, knowing who flies which reference buys under 1%, stacking the two classes apart costs 3% to 8% more, and widening every level costs 7.5% to 9% more, so the spacing stays at 13.3 m; the mismatch is swept, not sourced. 11ak sources it from a year of NOAA ISD airport pressure reports in New York (2014): a stale airport altimeter setting puts barometric drones 2.9 m (sd) off true pressure altitude, 4.2 m when the setting comes from an airport 18 km away, with heavy tails; under that measured mismatch the plan keeps 13.3 m spacing, mixing references costs 3.9% to 5.8% over one shared reference, and a Gaussian of the same sd gives the same plans. A barometer zeroed at take-off drifts 1.6 m over a 30-minute flight. The GNSS side’s own common error is not included. 11al shows that drones in the same pressure field share most of that drift (it cancels in their altitude gap): New York delivery missions last a median 3.4 min, the pressure part of the gap between two drones is about 0.55 m (mostly the hub-to-hub difference), and the stack keeps 13.3 m spacing at every mission length up to 60 min; treating the drift as independent per drone would widen it to 17.1 m and cost 12% more losses of separation. 11am sources the height-keeping noise from 17 public PX4 flight logs: the altitude controller holds its own estimate to 4.3 cm RMS, which alone would tighten the stack to 9.2 m (7 bands) and make the old 1 m assumption cost 5% to 8%; the barometer-minus-GNSS disagreement on the same flights (0.92 m) bounds the estimate’s own error, and at that bound the plan is 13.3 m again, so the decision turns on the barometer’s short-term error in forward flight. 11an measures it against RTK-fixed GNSS height in 7 public PX4 flights (of 400 logs, 98 with an RTK fix): barometric minus RTK altitude is a median 0.83 m RMS in level forward flight and 0.35 m in hover, mostly fast sensor noise (0.2 s correlation) but still 0.42 m (median) and 0.81 m (fleet RMS) after 5 s smoothing, with a speed-dependent static-pressure offset of about 1.4 m at 10 m/s; at that noise the planner keeps 13.3 m (5 bands) in 48 of 48 layouts and the 1 m assumption is optimal.. 11ao adds that static-pressure offset as an error that cancels inside an operator (one airframe, one speed) but not between operators: with offsets drawn from the 5 measured flights (−4.7 to +1.6 m at 10 m/s), the stack keeps 13.3 m (5 bands) and a plan that ignores them costs a median 2% to 3% (up to 73% in one draw); at twice the offset, a stand-in for faster cruise, it thins to 3 bands at 24 m and ignoring it costs 13% to 16%, while halving the offset by calibration removes the effect. 11ap reruns that with the offsets of all 12 flights spanning 5 m/s (−7.4 to +8.9 m): at the measured size the stack thins to 4 bands at 17.1 m and ignoring the offsets costs 15%, so the 5-band result depends on the flights chosen, while calibration to half keeps 5 bands under both; the 3-sigma spacing rule, fitted on per-drone noise, picks one to two bands too few when the per-operator offset dominates. 11aq to 11at test how the planner absorbs the offset: it keeps operators with similar offsets in neighbouring levels, no cheap rule (band sort, greedy insertion) matches it at the measured offset, and it needs only 10 to 20 random starts per spacing (within 1% of 200), the search costing about 3% of the CPU against the leak tables. Preliminary.
